To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the extent of forest fragmentation is increasing in the US, 2) the extent and rate of fragmentation is greatest in the eastern US, 3) fragmentation in the US is greatest in the southeastern US, 4) the extent of fragmentation varies by forest type and is greatest in the western US for conifer forests and in the southern US for hardwood forests, 5) the extent of large forest patches (>1000 ha) has decreased in the US, and 6)

the US forest landscape is highly fragmented (fragmentedness = 0.88) with a large proportion of the landscape in small forest patches (mean patch size 2.3 km ^{2} ), but with large areas of contiguous forest cover (mean core area size 1.2 million ha), especially in the northern and western US.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of landscape fragmentation on the distribution of species, and the implications for the design of conservation areas.
the effects of fragmentation on biodiversity, and the development and testing of tools to measure and monitor fragmentation.
the spatial pattern and connectivity of the US forested landscape, which has important implications for the conservation of biological diversity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the US has made great strides towards understanding and monitoring forest fragmentation, but there is still much work to do.
the results of the US assessments are encouraging but not conclusive.
there is no conclusive statement on the issue of national assessments of fragmentation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the US has a very fragmented forest landscape, with the majority of forested land occurring in relatively small patches.
the results of national assessments are useful for identifying areas where forest fragmentation is occurring and where further investigation is warranted.

landscape pattern is an important indicator of ecological integrity for forests and is amenable to quantification at national or multinational levels, and thus should be included in assessments of the ecological integrity of forests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, despite considerable challenges, it is possible to conduct national assessments of fragmentation and that such assessments may provide useful information for forest policy makers and land mangers.
the selection of an indicator of fragmentation is a complex process that requires careful consideration of the ecological context and the intended use of the indicator.
it is important to recognize that forest fragmentation is an ecological concept that cannot be measured directly and that it must be inferred from the spatial pattern of forest cover.
